title: Redis: distributed locks
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: SET NX EX, tokens, safe release with Lua, why replication breaks locks, Redlock and fencing tokens, and when to avoid a distributed lock at all.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

questions.prompt: What does SET lock:concert:343 my-token NX EX 30 do?

options.text: Creates the key only if it does not exist, with a 30 second expiry.
options.why: Right: success means you own the lock.

options.text: Overwrites the key and extends its life by 30 seconds.
options.why: NX prevents overwriting an existing key.

options.text: Reads the key and waits 30 seconds for it to appear.
options.why: It writes; it does not wait.

options.text: Locks the whole Redis instance for 30 seconds.
options.why: It only creates one key.

questions.explanation: NX gives mutual exclusion; EX stops a crashed holder from keeping the lock forever.

questions.prompt: Why put an expiry on the lock key?

options.text: So a crashed process cannot hold the lock forever.
options.why: Right: the key disappears on its own.

options.text: So the lock becomes faster to acquire.
options.why: Expiry does not change speed.

options.text: So other processes can read the lock holder's data.
options.why: Expiry has nothing to do with data access.

options.text: So Redis stores the key on disk.
options.why: Expiry is unrelated to persistence.

questions.explanation: Pick the expiry longer than the work and be ready for the case where it is not.

questions.prompt: Why store a random token and avoid a plain DEL when releasing?

options.text: DEL could remove a lock that another client now holds after yours expired.
options.why: Right: only release if the token still matches.

options.text: Tokens make the lock faster to acquire.
options.why: They matter for release, not speed.

options.text: DEL is not supported on keys with expiry.
options.why: DEL works on any key.

options.text: Tokens let replicas hold the lock too without any extra configuration.
options.why: Replicas do not take part.

questions.explanation: Check the token and delete in one atomic step.

questions.prompt: Why run the check-and-delete as a Lua script?

options.text: Redis runs the whole script as one command, so the check and delete are atomic.
options.why: Right: nothing can slip in between.

options.text: Lua is faster than any built-in command in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: The reason is atomicity, not raw speed.

options.text: Lua scripts persist the lock to disk.
options.why: Scripts do not affect durability.

options.text: Lua scripts bypass the single-thread model in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: They run on that single thread.

questions.explanation: A GET followed by a DEL from the client would leave a gap where the lock could change hands.

questions.prompt: A candidate calls the SET NX lock "optimistic locking". What is the correct correction?

options.text: It is pessimistic: you take the lock before doing the work.
options.why: Right: optimistic checks for conflicts at the end.

options.text: It is optimistic, because it uses an expiry as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Expiry does not make it optimistic.

options.text: It is neither, because Redis has no locking.
options.why: The lock is built from SET NX.

options.text: It is optimistic, because it never blocks anyone under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It makes others wait or retry.

questions.explanation: Redis also supports optimistic control: WATCH a key and run MULTI/EXEC; the transaction aborts if the key changed.

questions.prompt: How can a single-node Redis lock be granted twice?

options.text: The primary grants it, dies before replicating, and the promoted replica grants it again.
options.why: Right: asynchronous replication loses the key.

options.text: Two clients can both create the same key at once in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: NX makes creation atomic; only one wins.

options.text: The token is too short to be unique.
options.why: Random tokens are unique enough; that is not the failure.

options.text: Redis forgets the key when the TTL is too long in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: A long TTL keeps the key longer, not shorter.

questions.explanation: This is why a Redis lock is an efficiency tool that occasionally fails.

questions.prompt: What is the criticism of Redlock even though it uses a majority of nodes?

options.text: A paused or slow client can still act after its lock expired.
options.why: Right: timing assumptions can be broken.

options.text: It needs a majority of nodes, so it can never be used under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It can be used; the issue is its safety argument.

options.text: It stores locks in a relational database.
options.why: It uses several independent Redis nodes.

options.text: It removes expiries, so locks never release as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Locks still expire.

questions.explanation: A fencing token, a number that increases with each grant and is checked by the storage layer, defends against stale holders. Redis does not provide one.

questions.prompt: If a stale lock holder would corrupt your data, what is the better design?

options.text: Enforce the invariant where the data lives, for example a row lock or a conditional UPDATE with a version.
options.why: Right: the database makes the check atomic.

options.text: Raise the Redis lock expiry to several hours in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration in a typical production setup.
options.why: A long expiry does not stop stale holders.

options.text: Add more Redis replicas for the lock key for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: Async replicas do not give the guarantee.

options.text: Retry the lock acquisition more often.
options.why: Retries do not fix correctness.

questions.explanation: Or use a consensus system such as ZooKeeper or etcd. Treat a Redis lock as an efficiency tool.

questions.prompt: True or false: a SET NX EX lock needs no expiry because the holder always releases it.

options.text: True
options.why: It does need one.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the expiry covers crashed holders.

questions.explanation: Processes crash. Without an expiry, a dead holder would block everyone forever.
